issues.legal_issue: A witness may identify a closely acquainted person by voice in darkness, and that identification may support the conviction.
material_facts: The occurrence took place at night, when visual identification was difficult.
The eyewitness was closely related to and familiar with the accused.
The eyewitness recognized the accused by his voice when the accused spoke during the attack.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the challenge to the identification and held that the eyewitness’s recognition of the accused by voice could be relied on.
issues.legal_principle: In Anwar Hussain v. State of U.P. and Anr. (AIR 1981 SC 2073), the Court held that even in insufficient light a witness fairly acquainted or in intimate terms with a person may identify that person from voice, gait, or features.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and occurrence_in_darkness and witness_familiar_with_accused and accused_recognized_by_voice

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.occurrence_in_darkness: The relevant occurrence took place in darkness or insufficient light for easy visual identification.
predicates.witness_familiar_with_accused: The identifying witness was closely acquainted with the person identified.
predicates.accused_recognized_by_voice: The witness recognized the accused from the accused’s voice during the occurrence.

issues.definition: When a familiar witness recognizes an accused by voice during an occurrence in darkness, the voice identification may be relied on in an appeal against conviction.

issues.legal_issue: The acquittal of some accused does not require acquittal of another where the evidence against that person can be separated and assessed independently.
material_facts: The eyewitness identified one assailant but did not identify the other assailants.
The other accused were acquitted, while the evidence identifying the appellant as an assailant was accepted.
The Court considered whether the accepted portion of the eyewitness’s testimony could be separated from the portion insufficient to establish the guilt of the other accused.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal of the other accused did not require the appellant’s acquittal; the conviction could stand on the evidence accepted against him.
issues.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is not a rule of law in India but a rule of caution concerning the weight of evidence. A court must carefully screen the evidence and may separate reliable evidence from unreliable evidence; if truth and falsehood cannot be separated without reconstructing an entirely new case, the evidence must be discarded in toto. The Court relied on Nisar Alli v. State of Uttar Pradesh (AIR 1957 SC 366), Gurucharan Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1956 SC 460), Sahrab s/s Belli Nayata v. State of Madhya Pradesh ((1972) 3 SCC 751), Umar Ahir v. State of Bihar (AIR 1965 SC 277), Zwieolae Ariel v. State of Madhya Pradesh (AIR 1954 SC 15), Balaka Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1975 SC 1962), and State of Rajasthan v. Smt. Kalki (AIR 1981 SC 1390).

rule.if: multi_accused_criminal_case and appeal_against_conviction and some_coaccused_acquitted and evidence_against_appellant_separable and appellant_individually_identified

predicates.multi_accused_criminal_case: The criminal case involves multiple accused persons.
predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.some_coaccused_acquitted: One or more accused were acquitted while another accused was convicted.
predicates.evidence_against_appellant_separable: The evidence supporting the convicted accused can be separated from evidence insufficient to establish the guilt of others without reconstructing a new case.
predicates.appellant_individually_identified: The witness identified the convicted accused as an assailant.

issues.definition: In a criminal case involving multiple accused, the acquittal of some does not prevent a conviction from standing on appeal when the convicted accused was individually identified and the evidence against that accused is separable.
